description: The Four Noble Truths, nibbana, the Eightfold Path and the Threefold Way in Buddhism.
content_html:
The Four Noble Truths

After his enlightenment, the Buddha’s first formal teaching was the Four Noble Truths, delivered at the Deer Park at Isipatana and recorded in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. This sutta is the foundational text for the Four Noble Truths — Edexcel names it as the anchor source across all four truths.

The Four Noble Truths function like a medical diagnosis: identify the illness, find its cause, confirm a cure exists, and prescribe the treatment.

First Truth: Dukkha (Suffering)

The First Truth is that life involves dukkha — suffering, unsatisfactoriness. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta identifies three types: obvious physical and mental pain; the suffering caused by change (pleasant things pass away); and the subtle suffering of conditioned existence itself. This is not pessimism but an honest diagnosis. Recognising dukkha is the first step toward freedom from it.

Second Truth: Samudaya (The Cause of Suffering)

Samudaya means arising or origin. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta’s Sermon at Benares identifies the root of suffering as tanha (craving, thirst). Tanha fuels the Three Poisons: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). These three are depicted at the hub of the Wheel of Life as a pig, a snake and a cockerel — the three animals that pull all living beings around the cycle of rebirth.

Key Fact

The Three Poisons — greed (pig), hatred (snake) and delusion (cockerel) — are depicted at the centre of the Wheel of Life (Bhavachakra). They represent the root causes of tanha (craving), which is the Second Noble Truth’s explanation of why suffering arises. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is the named source for this teaching.

Theravada Buddhists treat the Wheel of Life as a map of the rebirth realms that beings cycle through due to kamma. The goal is to exit the wheel entirely by achieving nibbana. Mahayana Buddhists also use the Wheel but emphasise that the Bodhisattva freely enters the cycle of rebirth to assist others towards liberation. For Mahayana, the Three Poisons are not just personal obstacles but represent the delusions that affect all sentient beings. This divergence means a Mahayana Buddhist may engage with the world differently than a Theravada monk who withdraws from it.

Third Truth: Nirodha (Cessation)

Nirodha means cessation or stopping. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta teaches that suffering can end: when tanha is completely extinguished, nibbana (nirvana in Sanskrit) is reached. Nibbana literally means ‘blowing out’ — as a flame is extinguished — but it is not simple nothingness. It is the end of conditioned suffering and the cessation of the causes that keep beings bound to samsara (the cycle of rebirth).

Key Fact

Nibbana (Third Noble Truth) is the goal of Buddhist practice. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, as the anchor text, records that the Buddha described it as the cessation of tanha and the end of rebirth in samsara. Theravada sees nibbana as the complete liberation of an individual; Mahayana sees it as encompassing all beings through the Bodhisattva path. This comparison point (1.5*) is important for 12-mark Discuss questions.

This spec point (1.5*) requires comparison with Christianity. Key contrasts: Buddhism teaches nibbana — the cessation of the causes of rebirth — whereas Christianity teaches resurrection of the body and eternal life with God (e.g. John 11:25). Buddhism’s cycle of samsara (multiple rebirths) contrasts with the Christian idea of one earthly life followed by judgement. Buddhism does not require a creator God for liberation; Christian salvation is achieved through faith in Christ. Both traditions affirm that the present life shapes what comes after it — Buddhist kamma and Christian moral living — but the mechanisms and goals differ fundamentally.

Fourth Truth: Magga (The Path)

Magga means path. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta teaches that the Middle Way — avoiding both extreme luxury and extreme self-denial — leads to nibbana. The specific path is the Eightfold Path: Right Understanding, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.

These eight aspects group into the Threefold Way: sila (ethical conduct: Right Speech, Action, Livelihood), samadhi (mental development: Right Effort, Mindfulness, Concentration) and panna (wisdom: Right Understanding, Intention). All three support each other — ethical behaviour creates the conditions for meditation, which in turn deepens wisdom.
exam_tip_html: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is your named source for all four Noble Truths — use it by name in your 5-mark answer. For ‘Explain two with sources’, name the Sutta and link it to a specific truth. The 12-mark Discuss question on this topic often focuses on which truth is ‘most important’ or whether nibbana is achievable — the 1.5* comparison-marked spec point requires you to contrast Buddhist nibbana with Christian afterlife beliefs. Develop the Christian side with at least one named source (e.g. John 11:25) to avoid the common error of leaving the alternative view as a single sentence. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of ‘Dhammacakkappavattana’, ‘samudaya’, ‘nirodha’ and ‘magga’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Four Noble Truths (dukkha, samudaya, nirodha, magga) form the core of the Buddha’s first teaching, recorded in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. They diagnose suffering, its cause (tanha/Three Poisons), its cure (nibbana) and the path (Eightfold Path).
  • Nibbana is the cessation of tanha and liberation from samsara; Theravada sees it as individual liberation, Mahayana extends it to all beings through the Bodhisattva ideal.
  • The Eightfold Path groups into the Threefold Way: sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation) and panna (wisdom) — all three aspects support each other in practice.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Four Noble Truths.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate, identified truths with a brief explanation. Dukkha: suffering/unsatisfactoriness exists; Samudaya: suffering has a cause (tanha/craving); Nirodha: suffering can cease (nibbana); Magga: there is a path to the cessation of suffering (the Eightfold Path / Middle Way).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Threefold Way in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Sila (ethical conduct) covers Right Speech, Right Action and Right Livelihood (1 mark). Samadhi (mental development/meditation) covers Right Effort, Mindfulness and Concentration (1 mark). Panna (wisdom) covers Right Understanding and Right Intention (1 mark). Development: the three support each other because ethical behaviour creates the conditions for meditation, which deepens wisdom (bonus development point, max 3).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Buddhist teachings about why suffering arises.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching (1 for identification, 2 for development). Teaching 1: tanha (craving) — the Second Noble Truth identifies craving for sensory pleasure, existence and non-existence as the root of suffering; clinging to things as permanent causes inevitable disappointment. Teaching 2: the Three Poisons (greed, hatred, delusion) — these are depicted at the centre of the Wheel of Life as driving beings through samsara; they fuel tanha and keep beings trapped in conditioned existence.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Buddhist beliefs about nibbana.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks for two developed explanations, +1 for naming the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Belief 1: nibbana is the cessation of tanha (craving) — when all craving is extinguished, the causes of suffering and rebirth in samsara end. Belief 2: nibbana differs between Theravada and Mahayana — Theravada sees it as individual liberation, while Mahayana Bodhisattvas delay personal nibbana to help all sentient beings. 5th mark: ‘The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta records the Buddha teaching nirodha — the cessation of tanha — as the Third Noble Truth.’

practice_questions.text:
'The Eightfold Path is the most important part of the Four Noble Truths.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; conclusion justifies a position. Arguments in support: the Eightfold Path is the practical prescription without which the other truths are just theory; it covers all aspects of life (ethics, meditation, wisdom) through the Threefold Way; it is the Middle Way that the Buddha himself followed to enlightenment. Arguments against: without understanding dukkha (First Truth) there is no motivation to practise; identifying tanha as the cause (Second Truth) diagnoses the specific problem the path addresses; nibbana as the goal (Third Truth) gives the path its meaning — without the destination the path is directionless; some argue that the Second Truth’s diagnosis of tanha is the most fundamental insight. Secure (7-9): Both sides with some development; Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Very brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three aspects of the Eightfold Path.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three correctly identified aspects. Any three from: Right Understanding, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration. Brief explanation earns the mark; full development is not required.

knowledge_checks.q: The Threefold Way groups the Eightfold Path into sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation) and _____ (wisdom).
The Three Poisons depicted at the centre of the Wheel of Life are greed, delusion and _____.
Match each Noble Truth to its Pali name:

flashcard_questions.a: The Sutta recording the Buddha's first teaching of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park.
The Second Noble Truth: the origin of suffering is tanha (craving).
Greed (lobha), hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) — the root causes of suffering.
The Third Noble Truth: the cessation of suffering through extinguishing tanha.
The Buddhist goal: liberation from samsara through the extinguishing of greed, hatred and delusion.
The cycle of death and rebirth beings are trapped in by craving and ignorance.
The path between extreme luxury and extreme self-denial, taught by the Buddha as the route to nibbana.
The Fourth Noble Truth: the Eightfold Path leading to nibbana.
Three divisions of the Eightfold Path: sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation), panna (wisdom).

flashcard_questions.q: How does Theravada nibbana differ from Mahayana nibbana?
flashcard_questions.a: Theravada: individual liberation. Mahayana: Bodhisattvas delay nibbana to liberate all beings.

flashcard_questions.q: What three animals represent the Three Poisons at the hub of the Wheel of Life?

glossary_terms.definition: The Buddha's core diagnosis of the human condition and its solution: suffering exists, it has a cause, it can cease, and there is a path to its cessation.
The 'First Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma' Sutta, containing the Buddha's first teaching of the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
The Second Noble Truth: the origin or cause of suffering is tanha (craving/thirst) and its related mental poisons.
Craving or thirst; the fundamental cause of suffering according to the Second Noble Truth.
The three root causes of suffering in Buddhism: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha), depicted at the hub of the Wheel of Life.
The Third Noble Truth: the cessation of suffering is possible through the complete ending of tanha.
The ultimate goal of Buddhism: the extinguishing of greed, hatred and delusion; liberation from the cycle of samsara.
The cycle of death and rebirth that beings are trapped in as long as they are driven by craving and ignorance.
The Fourth Noble Truth: the Middle Way path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering, consisting of the Eightfold Path.
The Buddha's practical guide to ethical and mental development leading to nibbana, consisting of eight interconnected aspects of right living.
The three divisions of the Eightfold Path: sila (ethical conduct), samadhi (mental development) and panna (wisdom).
The older Buddhist tradition emphasising individual liberation through monastic practice; predominant in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The broader Buddhist tradition including Pure Land, Zen and Tibetan forms, emphasising the Bodhisattva ideal and the liberation of all beings.
